subject: Biology
title: Mutualism: Evolving Together
description: A 60-second lesson on Mutualism: Evolving Together.

hook.text: Fig trees and fig wasps have co-evolved for 80 million years. Neither can survive without the other.

buildup.text: Each fig species has its own wasp species. The wasp pollinates the fig; the fig feeds the wasp's larvae.

discovery.text: Leafcutter ants farm specific fungus species. The fungus has lost the ability to survive without the ants.

twist.text: Mitochondria in your cells were once free-living bacteria. They merged with our ancestors 2 billion years ago.

climax.text: The deepest mutualisms blur the line between two organisms and one. Lichens are a fungus and an alga living as one.

punchline.text: Cooperation can be just as powerful as competition.

quiz.question: How long have fig trees and fig wasps co-evolved?

details.summary: Coevolved mutualisms develop when two species reciprocally adapt to each other over evolutionary time. From mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots to ants farming aphids, these partnerships show how cooperation can be as powerful a force in evolution as competition.
details.whyItMatters: Mutualistic coevolution has produced some of the most important relationships on Earth, including the plant-mycorrhiza partnership that enabled land colonization. These relationships sustain ecosystems and continue evolving today.
takeaways: Mycorrhizal fungi helped plants colonize land over 400 million years ago
Leaf-cutter ants farm fungal gardens in a 50-million-year-old mutualism
Mutualism can break down into parasitism if conditions change

faq.question: How do mutualistic relationships remain stable over evolution?
faq.answer: Sanctions and partner choice help maintain cooperation. Plants cut nutrient supply to fungal partners that provide poor services. Fig trees abort fruits with freeloading wasps. These enforcement mechanisms prevent cheating and stabilize the mutualism.

faq.question: Can mutualism evolve into parasitism?
faq.answer: Yes. If conditions change or enforcement breaks down, one partner can begin exploiting the other. Mycorrhizal fungi can become parasitic on nutrient-rich soils. Mutualism and parasitism exist on a continuum, with the balance depending on environmental conditions.
